sentenceSets.sentence: He was too much of an egotist to recognize when his involvement was making things worse rather than better.

answerChoices.reasoning: A narcissist craves admiration and is wounded by its absence, but the failure described is simpler: he cannot see past his own importance long enough to notice his effect on the work.
An egoist holds the doctrine that self-interest properly governs conduct, a philosophical position, whereas this man's problem is an inflated sense of his own centrality.
A braggart's fault lies in what he says about himself to others, while nothing here concerns his talk; the blind spot shows up in his judgment about when to stay involved.
A solipsist doubts that anything outside his own mind exists at all, an intellectual extreme far beyond a man who simply overrates his own contribution.
A perfectionist would scrutinize the results obsessively and so would be likelier to notice things getting worse, not less likely.
A meddler interferes in matters that are not his business, but the sentence assumes his involvement was legitimate and faults his inability to judge its effect.
An optimist misjudges outcomes generally, whereas his blindness attaches specifically to the value of his own participation.
An amateur lacks skill, which would explain poor work but not the inability to see that his presence was the problem.
An altruist attends to others' interests and would withdraw as soon as he saw he was harming the effort.
A pessimist would assume he was making things worse rather than fail to notice it.
A recluse avoids involvement entirely, so there would be nothing for him to misjudge.

sentenceSets.sentence: Every anecdote the egotist told somehow curved back to his own part in the events described.

answerChoices.reasoning: A boaster makes open claims about his achievements, but the sentence describes stories that are ostensibly about other things and quietly bend toward the teller.
Self-promotion is aimed at an advantage such as a job or a following, whereas nothing here suggests he is angling for anything beyond being the center of his own stories.
An exhibitionist courts shock and display, while these anecdotes are ordinary tales whose only peculiarity is where they end up.
A show-off performs a visible skill for an audience, but no stunt or talent is on view here; only the drift of every story toward himself.
A bore is defined by the effect on listeners, and the sentence comments on the pattern of the stories rather than on anyone's tedium.
A windbag talks at excessive length, but the fault noted is the destination of each anecdote, not its duration.
A raconteur is admired for telling stories well, a compliment the sentence's dry 'somehow' plainly withholds.
A gossip trades in other people's affairs, the reverse of stories that keep returning to the speaker.
A listener is not the one telling the anecdotes.
An ascetic renounces comfort and attention, which has nothing to do with the pattern in his storytelling.
A wallflower stays silent at the edge of the room rather than supplying every anecdote.

sentenceSets.sentence: A lifelong egotist, she treated every pause in the conversation as an invitation to return to her own affairs.

answerChoices.reasoning: An egomaniac is consumed by grandiose ideas of personal greatness, a pathological extreme beyond a woman who simply steers each lull back toward herself.
A self-dramatist stages her life as theater for effect, but the sentence records only that her own affairs are where every conversation ends up.
Attention-seeking implies contrivance to be noticed, whereas she needs no contrivance; she simply assumes the conversation belongs to her by default.
A prima donna is difficult and demanding about how she is treated, but no tantrums or demands appear here, only the reliable subject of her talk.
An extrovert is energized by company generally and might just as happily draw others out during a pause.
A chatterbox fills silence with talk of any kind, while what marks her is that the talk is always about herself.
An interrupter cuts across other speakers, but she waits for a pause, which is exactly not an interruption.
A monologuist holds the floor without pause, yet the sentence describes a conversation with silences she then fills.
An introvert would let the pause stand rather than seize it.
Cynicism is a view about other people's motives and says nothing about whose affairs get discussed.
A stoic is reticent about personal matters, the opposite of returning to them at every opportunity.
